newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss secrecy cloaks sick Mobutu, east Zaire flares.
newsitem.headline: Swiss secrecy cloaks sick Mobutu, east Zaire flares.

text.p: Concern is growing over the health of Zaire's stricken leader Mobutu Sese Seko on Wednesday as conflict spreads in the east of his chaotic Central African nation.
The two Swiss specialities of secrecy and quiet security surround the ailing 66-year-old president, reputed to be one of the world's richest men.
He has been undergoing cancer treatment for two months in this quiet Swiss town on the shores of Lake Geneva where his movements are a closely guarded secret.

As up to 250,000 Rwandan and Burundian refugees flee clashes between Zairean troops and ethnic Tutsis in eastern Zaire's Kivu region, Mobutu's prolonged absence has raised fears about what will happen in his vast, anarchic country if he dies.

Since undergoing surgery for prostate cancer on August 22 at Lausanne's University Hospital, Mobutu and his entourage of more than 20 aides and bodyguards have been living in the waterfront Beau-Rivage Palace hotel, one of the world's most exclusive.

Like a mini-government in exile, Mobutu has installed a Zairean telephone operator at the glamorous, neo-Baroque hotel. Asked about his calls, a receptionist said: "We don't deal with their calls. They have their own telephone operator. A Zairean."
Hotel staff say they rarely see Mobutu but his presence is felt everywhere inside the Beau-Rivage, inaugurated in 1861 and where Coco Chanel and Somerset Maugham used to holiday.

A visiting correspondent on Tuesday found Zairean bodyguards clutching mobile phones roaming the corridors. Mobutu and his team -- referred to by hotel staff as "le delegation" -- have taken inter-connected suites on the top floor. Prices start from 1,500 Swiss Francs ($1,188) a night.
Zairean security guards said the president was holidaying in the nearby mountain resort of Interlaken.
When Mobutu, who stands six feet (1.8 metres) tall, ventures out, he goes out with groups of 20 or more aides and is noticeable by his trademark leopardskin fur hat, witnesses say.
There have been reports of rare sightings at gourmet restaurants in Lausanne and at the University Hospital.
"He was here last week, wearing his fur hat," said a hospital receptionist. "He's a very impressive man, he's always surrounded by a crowd."
"Absolutely no comment. This is secret," was the response from hospital officials to questions about Mobutu's health.
The former journalist-turned-soldier who seized power in 1965 after five years of civil war, is widely regarded as having presided over an increasingly corrupt administration.

Bloodshed and rebellion have marked mineral-rich Zaire since independence from Belgium in 1960. Chief exports have included copper, cobalt, petroleum, diamonds, coffee, gold and manganese to major trading partners Belgium, West Germany, South Africa, the United States and France.

Swiss television said Mobutu, believed to have transferred large sums of money abroad during his long rule, had some $4 billion in banks in Switzerland -- about half of a reputed total of $8-10 billion in accounts around the world.
Residents say Zairean tensions spilled over into Lausanne's streets a month ago when Mobutu's exiled opponents demonstrated in front of the Beau-Rivage, chanting "Mobutu, assassin!"
A Swiss waiter in a nearby hotel complained that Mobutu was disturbing the tranquillity of serene Lausanne.
"He's a fat dictator and it's a disgrace we have him in our country," he said. "But what can we do? He's our client."
